slides.1: SDG 1 opens with an uncomfortable question. Can real poverty survive inside a developed society like Taiwan? It can, and it quietly decides how far a young person in this room is able to go.
slides.2: SDG 1 asks governments to end poverty in every form. That includes low income, unsafe housing and weak social protection. The goal treats poverty as a fault in the system, not a personal failure.
slides.3: Taiwan has strong education, health care and technology. Even so, inequality remains. A family can look normal from outside while carrying debt, nursing a sick parent, or living on work that could end tomorrow.
slides.4: Working poverty matters because hard work no longer brings security. Parents on temporary contracts lose the hours and the energy their children need. Poverty then travels into the next generation, and that is how it repeats.
slides.5: Housing costs create poverty quietly. Once the rent takes too much of the income, everything else has to be sacrificed. Students who move often or share a crowded room lose sleep, concentration and confidence.
slides.6: Digital access is now part of basic opportunity. Without a reliable device, a good connection and someone to ask, a student cannot fully join homework, research or AI learning. Their poverty is simply harder to see.
slides.7: Taiwan has built several safety nets: health insurance, social welfare, emergency relief and local service centers. These protect many people. However, good policy must be easy to find, simple to apply for and respectful to use.
slides.8: Schools are strong because they see students every day. Meal support, scholarships, counseling and after-school clubs take real weight off a family. A teacher who notices early becomes a bridge to local services.
slides.9: Local organizations often understand a neighborhood better than any ministry does. They provide food, tutoring, care and job news. Yet SDG 1 is not charity, because the goal is to give people choices, skills and dignity.
slides.10: Financial literacy gives you real power in daily life. Knowing about budgets, savings, debt, insurance and scams leads to better choices. Of course school cannot replace a fair wage, but it does build personal resilience.
slides.11: Data tools can reveal the poverty that nobody has counted. Students can map service locations, transport gaps or after-school resources, and a community then chooses more wisely. But every data point is still a real person.
slides.12: Service learning turns SDG 1 into real experience. Students can interview social workers, build bilingual guides or help with tutoring. Their English gets better as well, because they speak for a purpose, not for a grade.
slides.13: An aging society changes the shape of poverty. Older adults may live alone, manage illness, or struggle with services that have moved online. SDG 1 therefore connects welfare, transport, health care and community, not just income.
slides.14: Poverty is harder to escape for migrant workers and new immigrant families. Language and paperwork can build a wall around help. If the message is clear and multilingual, more people will ask for it.
slides.15: Climate risk is a poverty issue. When a disaster arrives, low-income families lose more and recover far more slowly. So shelters, insurance, clear advice and neighbors who check on each other have to be ready first.
slides.16: Dignity changes the way support is given. Poverty should never be treated as shame or laziness, because many people are strong and simply face unfair conditions. Respectful help asks people what they actually need.
slides.17: In summary, SDG 1 is not only about money. It is about whether everyone can live with safety and opportunity. Taiwan has clearly progressed, yet hidden poverty still asks us to improve access, timing and fairness.
slides.18: The most useful change may be our own language. Calling people lazy ends the conversation at once. Asking which barriers they meet opens it, because we then have to discuss wages, rent, health, transport and education.
slides.19: Students are not too young to act on this. They can run bilingual campaigns, volunteer, collect stories, design simple tools, or present their ideas to the school. PechaKucha turns private study into a public voice.
slides.20: Ending poverty sounds enormous, yet the action usually starts nearby. Notice a need, check the facts, speak respectfully and work with somebody else. If we connect English, the SDGs and action, students can become real changemakers.
